## The Loose Connection

At 4:12 on a Tuesday morning, the radiator began speaking in my grandfather’s voice.

Not clearly at first. It made its usual noises: the tick of expanding metal, the long abdominal gurgle that had once caused me, aged six, to ask whether the house was digesting us. Then it said, quite distinctly, “Mind the paint.”

I sat up.

My grandfather had been dead for eleven years. Before that, he had been alive for eighty-three, and for most of them he had behaved as if the world were a recently assembled appliance whose instructions had been misplaced. He repaired wireless sets, umbrellas, the church gate, a neighbour’s marriage—temporarily—and my bicycle, which never worked properly again but did so with tremendous character.

“Mind the paint” was what he said whenever anyone knocked against anything. It was also what he said when my grandmother reversed into the garden wall, when my mother announced she was moving to Glasgow, and when I told him, at seventeen, that I wanted to study philosophy.

“There’s no paint here,” I said.

The radiator knocked twice.

“Don’t be clever at this hour,” it replied.

I turned on the bedside lamp. The room looked insultingly ordinary: socks on the floor, cold cup on the windowsill, the wallpaper my grandmother had chosen because it hid damp and, she claimed, sins.

“Grandad?”

“You’ll wake the house.”

“I live alone.”

“Then you’ve no excuse.”

This was so exactly the sort of answer he would have given that I laughed. The laugh became something else halfway through, and I put a hand over my mouth until it stopped.

I had moved back six weeks earlier, after my marriage ended, with two suitcases and a lamp I didn’t like. The house had been his, then my mother’s, then, through solicitors and a great deal of tea, mine. Everyone called it a fresh start. It felt more like being returned to the shop.

“Fetch the spanners,” said the radiator.

“Why?”

“Because talking to you is giving me a headache.”

The toolbox was under the sink. I knew because I had put it there myself, unable to throw it away and unable to look at it. Inside lay the blunt diplomacy of his life: screwdrivers with split handles, three kinds of pliers, screws saved in tobacco tins, and a folded paper on which he had written, in pencil, IF IN DOUBT, TIGHTEN IT GENTLY.

“What am I tightening?”

“Valve. Other end. Not that end. Are you trying to drown us?”

For ten minutes I worked while he insulted my hands. Water hissed. Air sighed out. A smell of dust and rust rose from the carpet. It was the closest I had come to peace since September.

When I finished, I sat on the floor with my back against the bed.

“I meant to come that Christmas,” I said.

The pipes ticked.

“I kept thinking there would be a quieter week. Then there was the hospital, and then Mum said you were sleeping, and I thought—I don’t know what I thought. That you’d know. That I’d get another chance to be useful.”

“You were never useful,” he said. “You were loved. Different department.”

Outside, a milk float passed, though I hadn’t seen a milk float in years. Somewhere a bird tried one note and thought better of it.

“Why now?” I asked.

“You were making such a row.”

“I wasn’t.”

“Not out loud.”

I looked at the radiator. Its white paint was yellowed around the brackets. One of my grandmother’s hair grips was still wedged beneath it, a fact that seemed, suddenly, almost unbearable.

“Does it stop?” I said.

“What?”

“This.”

“Ah,” he said. “That.”

I waited.

“Some things you mend,” he said at last. “Some things you keep company while they’re broken. People get muddled and try to do the second job with the first set of tools.”

“That’s not much of a philosophy.”

“You’re the philosopher.”

The sky behind the curtains had begun to turn the colour of weak tea. His voice was fading, not growing quieter exactly, but returning to the sounds around it: water, metal, the small shifts of a house warming up.

“Will you come back?” I asked.

“Bleed me in winter. Ring your mother. And buy a decent kettle.”

“Grandad?”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Good,” he said. “You’re learning.”

Then the radiator only gurgled.

I sat there until the sun reached the toolbox. After a while I went downstairs, filled a saucepan with water because the kettle was, in fact, leaking, and rang my mother. She answered on the first ring, as if she had been awake for hours.

“I was just thinking about you,” she said.

“Are you all right?” I asked.

“I was going to ask you that.”

I looked up the stairs. From the bedroom came the faint, contented ticking of warm metal.

“No,” I said, surprising us both. “But the radiator’s fixed.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“I’ll bring bread,” she said.

Behind me, in the hall, something clicked twice. It could have been the pipes. It could have been an old man telling me to mind the paint.

I put two cups on the tray.

Not clearly at first. It made its usual noises: the tick of expanding metal, the long abdominal gurgle that had once caused me, aged six, to ask whether the house was digesting us. Then it said, quite distinctly, "Mind the paint."

I sat up.

My grandfather had been dead for eleven years. Before that, he had been alive for eighty-three, and for most of them he had behaved as if the world were a recently assembled appliance whose instructions had been misplaced. He repaired wireless sets, umbrellas, the church gate, a neighbour's marriage—temporarily—and my bicycle, which never worked properly again but did so with tremendous character.

"Mind the paint" was what he said whenever anyone knocked against anything. It was also what he said when my grandmother reversed into the garden wall, when my mother announced she was moving to Glasgow, and when I told him, at seventeen, that I wanted to study philosophy.

"There's no paint here," I said.

The radiator knocked twice.

"Don't be clever at this hour," it replied.

I turned on the bedside lamp. The room looked insultingly ordinary: socks on the floor, cold cup on the windowsill, the wallpaper my grandmother had chosen because it hid damp and, she claimed, sins.

"Grandad?"

"You'll wake the house."

"I live alone."

"Then you've no excuse."

This was so exactly the sort of answer he would have given that I laughed. The laugh became something else halfway through, and I put a hand over my mouth until it stopped.

I had moved back six weeks earlier, after my marriage ended, with two suitcases and a lamp I didn't like. The house had been his, then my mother's, then, through solicitors and a great deal of tea, mine. Everyone called it a fresh start. It felt more like being returned to the shop.

"Fetch the spanners," said the radiator.

"Why?"

"Because talking to you is giving me a headache."

The toolbox was under the sink. I knew because I had put it there myself, unable to throw it away and unable to look at it. Inside lay the blunt diplomacy of his life: screwdrivers with split handles, three kinds of pliers, screws saved in tobacco tins, and a folded paper on which he had written, in pencil, IF IN DOUBT, TIGHTEN IT GENTLY.

"What am I tightening?"

"Valve. Other end. Not that end. Are you trying to drown us?"

For ten minutes I worked while he insulted my hands. Water hissed. Air sighed out. A smell of dust and rust rose from the carpet. It was the closest I had come to peace since September.

When I finished, I sat on the floor with my back against the bed.

"I meant to come that Christmas," I said.

The pipes ticked.

"I kept thinking there would be a quieter week. Then there was the hospital, and then Mum said you were sleeping, and I thought—I don't know what I thought. That you'd know. That I'd get another chance to be useful."

"You were never useful," he said. "You were loved. Different department."

Outside, a milk float passed, though I hadn't seen a milk float in years. Somewhere a bird tried one note and thought better of it.

"Why now?" I asked.

"You were making such a row."

"I wasn't."

"Not out loud."

I looked at the radiator. Its white paint was yellowed around the brackets. One of my grandmother's hair grips was still wedged beneath it, a fact that seemed, suddenly, almost unbearable.

"Does it stop?" I said.

"What?"

"This."

"Ah," he said. "That."

I waited.

"Some things you mend," he said at last. "Some things you keep company while they're broken. People get muddled and try to do the second job with the first set of tools."

"That's not much of a philosophy."

"You're the philosopher."

The sky behind the curtains had begun to turn the colour of weak tea. His voice was fading, not growing quieter exactly, but returning to the sounds around it: water, metal, the small shifts of a house warming up.

"Will you come back?" I asked.

"Bleed me in winter. Ring your mother. And buy a decent kettle."

"Grandad?"

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good," he said. "You're learning."

Then the radiator only gurgled.

I sat there until the sun reached the toolbox. After a while I went downstairs, filled a saucepan with water because the kettle was, in fact, leaking, and rang my mother. She answered on the first ring, as if she had been awake for hours.

"I was just thinking about you," she said.

Behind me, in the hall, something clicked twice. It could have been the pipes. It could have been an old man telling me to mind the paint.

I put two cups on the tray.
